_source: Curated from widely published marine aquarium husbandry guidance, 2026-09-30; not FishBase

Amphiprion ocellaris.notes: Captive-bred fish are hardy and do not need an anemone. Keep a single pair; adding more clowns later usually leads to fighting.

Amphiprion percula.notes: Care matches the ocellaris; choose captive-bred fish. Keep a single pair per tank.

Amphiprion biaculeatus.notes: The most aggressive common clownfish; females grow large and dominate their area of the tank. Add it last and avoid other clownfish.

Chrysiptera parasema.temperament: Semi-aggressive, one of the milder damsels
Chrysiptera parasema.notes: Hardy and small, but still a damsel; it can harass new or smaller fish. Provide rockwork with hiding places.

Chromis viridis.notes: Kept in groups, which need open swimming room; groups often dwindle as dominant fish bully the weakest. Feed small meals several times a day.

Dascyllus aruanus.temperament: Aggressive and territorial as it matures
Dascyllus aruanus.notes: Very hardy, but adults defend a coral head or rock and chase tankmates. Hard to remove from a reef once established.

Zebrasoma flavescens.notes: Needs a long tank with swimming room and a steady supply of marine algae (nori). Quarantine before adding; tangs are prone to ich and HLLE.

Paracanthurus hepatus.temperament: Peaceful with most fish; may spar with other tangs
Paracanthurus hepatus.notes: Grows to about 30 cm and needs a long tank with rockwork to wedge into. Very ich-prone, so quarantine carefully and feed algae plus meaty foods.

Acanthurus leucosternon.notes: Notoriously ich-prone and stress-sensitive; needs careful quarantine, high oxygen and very stable water. Add it to a mature tank with plenty of algae to graze.

Zebrasoma xanthurum.notes: One of the more combative Zebrasoma tangs, so add it last among tangs. Needs algae in the diet and swimming room.

Centropyge loriculus.temperament: Semi-aggressive; keep one dwarf angel per tank
Centropyge loriculus.notes: Needs mature live rock to graze. May nip at LPS corals and clam mantles, so it is reef safe only with caution.

Centropyge bispinosa.temperament: Semi-aggressive; keep one dwarf angel per tank
Centropyge bispinosa.notes: One of the hardier dwarf angels; grazes on live rock. Some individuals pick at soft and LPS corals.

Pomacanthus imperator.temperament: Semi-aggressive; aggressive toward other large angels
Pomacanthus imperator.notes: Reaches about 40 cm, so it needs a very large fish-only tank with mature rock. Feed a varied diet that includes sponge-based foods; not reef safe.

Gramma loreto.notes: Hardy and reef safe; needs caves or overhangs to hover in. Keep one per tank unless the tank is large, and use a lid because it can jump.

Pseudochromis fridmani.temperament: Semi-aggressive, the mildest of the dottybacks
Pseudochromis fridmani.notes: Usually captive-bred and very hardy; needs rockwork with hiding places. Keep one per tank and avoid similar-shaped small fish.

Synchiropus splendidus.notes: Needs an established tank (six months or more) with a large copepod population, ideally supported by a mature refugium; many starve without it. Keep one male per tank and avoid fast competing feeders.

Elacatinus oceanops.notes: Widely captive-bred and short-lived (about one to two years). Accepts prepared foods and picks parasites from other fish.

Nemateleotris magnifica.notes: An accomplished jumper, so a tight-fitting lid is essential. Keep singly or as a mated pair and avoid boisterous tankmates.

Amblygobius phalaena.notes: Needs a large, mature sand bed to sift, plus supplemental feeding; it often slowly starves in small or new tanks. Can jump.

Salarias fasciatus.temperament: Peaceful with most fish; keep one per tank
Salarias fasciatus.notes: Depends on film algae and often starves once a tank's algae is gone; offer nori or algae-based foods. Intolerant of other blennies.

Ecsenius bicolor.notes: Hardy omnivore that grazes algae and takes prepared foods. Occasionally nips at LPS corals and clams.

Pterapogon kauderni.notes: Endangered in the wild, so buy captive-bred fish, which are far hardier. A male mouthbroods the eggs and fry can be raised on small foods.

Sphaeramia nematoptera.notes: Hardy and calm; keep in a small group with peaceful tankmates. Most active at dusk, so feed when lights dim if it hangs back.

Pterois volitans.temperament: Predator; swallows fish and shrimp that fit in its mouth
Pterois volitans.notes: Dorsal spines are venomous, so handle maintenance with care. Wean onto frozen meaty foods instead of live feeder fish.

Labroides dimidiatus.notes: Feeds on parasites and mucus of other fish and rarely thrives in aquariums, often starving within months. Many hobbyists recommend leaving it on the reef.

Halichoeres chrysus.notes: Needs a sand bed of at least 5 cm to bury in at night. Hunts small pests such as flatworms; keep a lid on the tank because wrasses jump.

Pseudanthias squamipinnis.temperament: Peaceful schooling fish; one male per group
Pseudanthias squamipinnis.notes: An active planktivore that needs several small feedings a day. Keep one male with several females in a large tank with open swimming room.

Chelmon rostratus.notes: Often hard to wean onto frozen foods; add it to a mature tank and start with live or fresh foods. Eats Aiptasia but may also pick at tube worms and some corals.

Hippocampus kuda.notes: Best in a tall species tank with gentle flow and hitching posts; buy captive-bred fish trained on frozen mysis. Keeping it on the cooler side lowers bacterial infection risk.

Siganus vulpinus.temperament: Peaceful; may spar with other rabbitfish
Siganus vulpinus.notes: Hardy algae grazer that needs plenty of vegetable matter. Its fin spines are venomous, so handle with care.

Oxycirrhites typus.notes: Perches on rock and gorgonians and eats small shrimp and very small fish. Keep a lid on the tank because it can jump.

Canthigaster valentini.notes: Offer hard-shelled foods such as clams and snails to keep its beak worn down. Nips at invertebrates, corals and slow fish.

Opistognathus aurifrons.notes: Needs a sand bed at least 8 to 10 cm deep with mixed grain sizes and rubble to build a burrow. A notorious jumper, so a tight-fitting lid is essential.
